title: Protein Plots
text:
The Protein Plots section allows individual proteins to be selected for detailed visualization of their thermal abundance profiles.
Protein selection is performed independently for each dataset, allowing proteins from different experimental conditions to be selected and subsequently compared.
The main steps are:

title: Protein Plots
text:
Protein selection
The Protein Selection table displays the proteins available in the currently active dataset.






Figure 1: Protein Selection table.



Each row represents a protein.
The first column contains the protein identifier, while the remaining columns contain the quantitative measurements associated with the different temperatures and replicates.
When clustering information is available, the table also contains the cluster assigned to each protein.






NoteData source



If clustering has not been performed, the Protein Selection table uses the current normalized dataset.
If clustering results are available, the corresponding cluster assignments are incorporated into the protein table.

title: Protein Plots
text:
Protein abundance measurements
The quantitative columns are organized according to:

Temperature
Replicate

For example, measurements may be displayed in an order such as:
40_REP1
40_REP2
43_REP1
43_REP2
46_REP1
46_REP2
This arrangement facilitates comparison of replicate measurements at the same temperature.






TipUsing cluster assignments



When clustering has already been performed, use the Cluster column to identify proteins belonging to a thermal-profile group of interest before generating individual protein plots.

title: Protein Plots
text:
Condition-specific protein tables
Protein selection is performed within the currently active condition or dataset.
Switching to another condition displays the protein table corresponding to that condition.
This allows proteins to be selected independently across experimental conditions.






ImportantSelections are condition-specific



Protein selections in the Protein Plots workflow are associated with the active condition.
This makes it possible to select proteins from one condition, switch to another condition, and make additional selections for comparison.

title: Protein Plots
text:
Comparison clustering results
When the Clustering module has been used in Condition comparison mode, the clustering result can contain measurements from multiple datasets.
In the Protein Selection interface, TPP Analyst displays the measurements corresponding to the relevant active dataset while retaining the cluster assignment obtained from the comparison analysis.
This makes it possible to inspect a protein within an individual condition while retaining information about the cluster assigned from its combined multi-condition thermal profile.

title: Protein Plots
section: Searching and filtering the protein table
text:
Searching and filtering the protein table
The Protein Selection table provides column-specific filters.
These filters can be used to restrict the displayed proteins according to identifiers, cluster assignments, or quantitative measurements.

Filtering protein identifiers
Text columns can be searched using character matching.
This is particularly useful for locating specific protein accessions.
For example, entering a protein accession in the corresponding filter field restricts the displayed table to matching proteins.


Filtering by cluster
When a Cluster column is present, the table can be filtered to proteins belonging to a particular cluster.
This provides a convenient way to inspect and select individual members of a thermal-profile group identified during clustering.


Filtering quantitative measurements
Numeric columns can be filtered using numeric values or comparison operators.
Supported comparisons include:
>value
>=value
<value
<=value
!=value
For example:
>1
can be used to restrict a quantitative column to proteins with measurements greater than 1.
Similarly:
<=0.5
restricts the table to proteins with measurements equal to or below 0.5 in the selected column.






TipCombining table filters



Filters can be applied to multiple columns to progressively narrow the table to proteins matching the desired characteristics.
For example, cluster membership can be combined with quantitative filters to identify proteins from a specific cluster that display particular abundance values.

title: Protein Plots
text:
Selecting proteins
One or more proteins can be selected directly from the table.
Click the desired rows to add them to the current selection.
Multiple rows can be selected simultaneously.
After selecting the proteins of interest, click:
Plot selected proteins






Figure 2: Protein plotting.









TipSelecting multiple proteins



Selecting several proteins at once is useful when comparing proteins displaying related thermal behaviors, proteins assigned to the same cluster, or a set of proteins of biological interest.

title: Protein Plots
text:
Plot selected proteins
The:
Plot selected proteins
button triggers visualization of the proteins currently selected from the active dataset.
Protein selections from different conditions can be combined through the broader Protein Plots workflow, allowing thermal abundance profiles to be compared across datasets.






Figure 3: Protein plotting comparison between conditions.



The protein-selection table itself therefore serves as the interface between the processed datasets and the downstream protein-level visualization.

title: Protein Plots
text:
Clearing the current selection
Click:
Clear selection
to remove the currently selected proteins from the active protein table.
This clears the selection without modifying the underlying protein dataset.






NoteClear selection



Clear selection affects only the current protein selection.
The function does not remove proteins from the normalized dataset, clustering results, or any previous analysis step.

title: Protein Plots
text:
Switching between datasets
When the available data source changes, TPP Analyst updates the protein table to reflect the appropriate dataset.
For example, the table may use:

the normalized protein dataset before clustering;
the clustered dataset after clustering has been performed.

Selections that no longer correspond to the active data source are cleared automatically to prevent mismatched protein selections.

title: Protein Plots
text:
Downloading the protein table
Click:
Download table
to export the protein table for the currently active condition as a CSV file.
The export corresponds to the condition currently displayed in the Protein Selection interface.

title: Protein Plots
text:
Recommended protein-selection workflow
A typical Protein Plots workflow is:

Select the experimental condition of interest.
Inspect the available protein table.
Use the accession filter to locate specific proteins when required.
Use the Cluster column when clustering information is available.
Apply quantitative filters if a specific abundance pattern is of interest.
Select one or more proteins from the table.
Click Plot selected proteins.
Switch to another condition when a cross-condition comparison is required.
Select additional proteins from that condition.
Generate the desired protein-level visualization.
Use Clear selection when the current active-condition selection should be reset.
Download the filtered protein table when required.







TipLinking clustering and protein-level inspection



A useful workflow is to first identify interesting thermal-profile groups in the Clustering module and then use the Cluster column in Protein Plots to inspect individual proteins belonging to those groups.

title: Protein Plots
Protein Plots
text:
Next step
After inspecting individual protein profiles, continue to GO Analysis for functional interpretation of selected protein groups.

title: Quality Control
text:
The Quality Control module provides tools for assessing, filtering, and preparing protein abundance data before normalization and downstream analysis.
Quality control is performed independently for each processed dataset. The module focuses on three main aspects of the data:
Filtering decisions made in this section determine which proteins are retained for subsequent analysis.

title: Quality Control
text:
Missing values
TPP Analyst reports the initial percentage of missing values before missing-value handling is applied.
The calculation considers the quantitative measurements and identifies the following values as missing:

NA
NaN
Inf

The percentage shown at this stage represents the original level of missing data in the dataset.






Figure 1: Condition tab selection and initial percentage of missing values.

title: Quality Control
text:
Handling missing values
TPP Analyst provides three strategies for handling missing values:

Remove all rows with any missing values
Impute all missing values
Remove all rows containing only missing values and impute the rest

Select the desired strategy and then click Apply transformation.






ImportantApply the transformation



The selected missing-value strategy is not applied until Apply transformation is clicked.
The transformed dataset is then used by the subsequent quality-control steps.



Remove all rows with any missing values
The Remove all rows with any missing values option removes a protein if at least one quantitative measurement for that protein is missing.
This represents the most restrictive missing-value strategy because only proteins with complete quantitative profiles are retained.






WarningComplete-case filtering



This option can remove a substantial number of proteins from datasets containing frequent missing measurements. Check the resulting number of retained proteins before continuing.




Impute all missing values
The Impute all missing values option retains proteins and replaces missing quantitative measurements using the selected imputation method.
TPP Analyst provides four imputation methods:

All to 0
min
knn
MLE



Remove all rows containing only missing values and impute the rest
The Remove all rows containing only missing values and impute the rest option combines filtering and imputation.
Proteins containing no observed quantitative measurements are removed first.
Remaining proteins containing both observed and missing measurements are retained, and their missing values are estimated using the selected imputation method.
This option can be useful when completely unobserved proteins should be excluded while partially observed proteins should remain available for subsequent analysis.

title: Quality Control
text:
Imputation methods
When Impute all missing values or Remove all rows containing only missing values and impute the rest is selected, an imputation method must also be chosen.

All to 0
The All to 0 method replaces each missing quantitative measurement with zero.
This approach does not estimate a value from other proteins or measurements. Instead, missing observations are explicitly represented as zero.
Because zero values can subsequently be examined and filtered within the QC module, the effect of this transformation can be assessed using the zero-value visualizations and filters described below.


Minimum-value imputation
The min method replaces missing measurements using the minimum observed value within the corresponding quantitative column.
This retains proteins containing missing measurements while assigning those observations a low abundance value based on the observed data.


K-nearest neighbour imputation
The knn option performs K-nearest neighbour imputation.
TPP Analyst uses the available quantitative profiles to estimate missing measurements from similar proteins.
Proteins containing only missing quantitative values cannot contribute useful information to this procedure and are removed when necessary before KNN imputation is performed.


Maximum-likelihood estimation
The MLE option uses maximum-likelihood-based imputation to estimate missing quantitative measurements.
Negative values produced during the imputation procedure are converted to zero before the transformed dataset is used downstream.






WarningMLE and large datasets



MLE imputation is disabled when the quantitative dataset contains more than 3,000 proteins.
For datasets above this threshold, select another imputation method.

title: Quality Control
text:
Zero values
After missing-value handling has been applied, TPP Analyst evaluates zero values in the transformed dataset.
The Percentage of Zero Values indicator reports the percentage of quantitative measurements equal to zero in the current filtered dataset.
Unlike the initial missing-value percentage, this value can change when QC filters are adjusted.






NoteMissing values and zero values are treated separately



Missing-value handling is performed first. Zero values are subsequently evaluated and filtered using the transformed dataset.
For example, selecting All to 0 during imputation converts missing observations into zero values, which can then be inspected and filtered in the zero-value QC section.

title: Quality Control
text:
Filtering proteins by zero values
When zero values are present, TPP Analyst provides a slider for controlling how many zero measurements can be present in an individual protein profile.
The control is labelled:
Filter out proteins with number of zero values >= to:
Reducing the threshold progressively removes proteins containing larger numbers of zero measurements.
This provides a direct way to exclude sparsely quantified proteins before normalization and downstream analysis.
If the dataset contains no zero values, this filter is not displayed.

title: Quality Control
text:
Filtering proteins by average intensity
TPP Analyst also provides an average-intensity range filter.
The intensity for each protein is calculated using its positive quantitative measurements. Zero measurements are excluded when calculating the protein average.
The label of the filter depends on the preprocessing state of the dataset:

Average log2 intensity for data that have not already been scaled;
Average intensity for data already provided on a log2 scale;
Average normalized abundance for data that have already been normalized.

Both the lower and upper limits can be adjusted.
Proteins with average values outside the selected range are removed from the current filtered dataset.






Figure 2: Zero values percentage and slider filters.









TipIntensity filtering



The intensity range can be used to exclude very low- or very high-abundance proteins when these proteins are not appropriate for the intended downstream analysis.
Adjust the range while inspecting the QC visualizations and the number of retained proteins.

title: Quality Control
text:
Filter summary
Below the filtering controls, TPP Analyst reports:

Proteins retained
Proteins removed

The number of retained proteins is updated according to the current zero-value and intensity filters.
Use this information to assess how strongly the selected QC thresholds affect the size of the dataset.






ImportantCheck protein retention



Before proceeding to normalization, verify that the selected QC thresholds have not unintentionally removed a large proportion of the proteins required for the analysis.

title: Quality Control
text:
Distribution of zero values
The Distribution of zero values heatmap provides an overview of protein abundance patterns and the distribution of zero measurements across the dataset.
Each row represents a protein and each column represents a quantitative measurement.
Abundance is represented using a color scale ranging from low to high protein intensity.






Figure 3: Distribution of zero values heatmap.



The display can be customized using several controls.

Display mode
Two display modes are available:

Clustered
Per replicate

These options change how the quantitative columns are arranged in the heatmap.
Clustered organizes the measurements primarily according to temperature.
Per replicate organizes measurements primarily according to replicate and then temperature.
This allows the same dataset to be inspected from complementary perspectives.


Protein ordering
Proteins can be ordered using:

Clustering
Average intensity

When Clustering is selected, proteins are ordered according to similarities in their abundance profiles.
When Average intensity is selected, proteins are ordered according to their average abundance, calculated from non-zero measurements.
The average-intensity view also displays an intensity reference alongside the heatmap.


Show only proteins with zero values
The Show only proteins with zero values option restricts the heatmap to proteins containing at least one zero measurement.
This option is enabled by default and focuses the visualization specifically on proteins affected by zero values.
Disable the option to include proteins without zero measurements in the heatmap.






TipInspecting zero-value patterns



The heatmap is particularly useful for determining whether zero values are distributed broadly across the experiment or concentrated in particular proteins, temperatures, or replicates.

title: Quality Control
text:
Density plots of average intensity
The Density plots of average intensity visualization shows the distribution of protein abundance in the currently filtered dataset.
The abundance scale depends on the preprocessing state of the input data.
For unscaled datasets, abundance is displayed on a log2 scale. Data already marked as log2 transformed or normalized are displayed using their existing scale.
The density plot updates when the zero-value or average-intensity filters are changed.
This plot can help assess how the selected filtering thresholds affect the overall abundance distribution and is particullarly useful to compare the intensity distribution of proteins containing zero values with the distribution of proteins without zero values.






Figure 4: Density plots of average intensity.

title: Quality Control
section: Average number of zero values per temperature
text:
Average number of zero values per temperature
The Average number of zero values per temperature plot summarizes the occurrence of zero values across the thermal gradient.
For each temperature, the plot displays the average number of zero measurements together with their variation.
This visualization can be used to identify temperatures at which zero measurements are more frequent.
Such patterns may be particularly relevant at higher temperatures, where protein abundance can decrease as thermal destabilization progresses.






Figure 5: Average number of zero values per temperature.

title: Quality Control
text:
Total abundance plot
The Total abundance plot summarizes the total measured protein abundance at each temperature.
Quantitative measurements are combined by temperature, and the resulting total abundance is displayed across the thermal gradient.
This provides a dataset-level view of how the overall quantitative signal changes with temperature.






Figure 6: Total abundance plot.









NoteInterpreting QC plots together



No single QC visualization should be considered in isolation.
The zero-value percentage, heatmap, intensity distribution, zero values per temperature, total abundance profile, and number of retained proteins provide complementary information about the effect of the selected QC settings.

title: Quality Control
text:
Recommended QC workflow
A typical quality-control workflow in TPP Analyst is:

Inspect the initial percentage of missing values.
Choose how missing values should be handled.
Select an imputation method when required.
Click Apply transformation.
Inspect the resulting percentage of zero values.
Examine the zero-value heatmap and density distribution.
Inspect zero values across temperatures and the total abundance profile.
Adjust the zero-value threshold if necessary.
Adjust the average-intensity range if necessary.
Check how many proteins are retained and removed.
Reassess the QC visualizations after filtering.
Proceed to normalization when the filtered dataset is satisfactory.







ImportantQC decisions affect downstream analysis



Proteins removed by the QC filters are excluded from subsequent processing. Review the retained protein count and QC visualizations before continuing.

title: Quality Control
text:
Next step
Once missing values have been handled and the quality-control filters have been reviewed, continue to Normalization.

title: Normalization
text:
The Normalization module prepares the quality-controlled protein abundance data for downstream analysis.
TPP Analyst provides several normalization strategies that can be applied individually or in combination. The module also provides diagnostic visualizations for assessing sample distributions, global protein trends, sample similarity, potential outliers, and replicate variability.
The main steps of the normalization workflow are:

title: Normalization
text:
Normalization settings
TPP Analyst provides four normalization options:

log2 transformation
Within replicate median normalization
Reference protein normalization
Normalize to lowest temperature

One or more methods can be selected before clicking Apply selected normalization.






Figure 1: Normalization settings.



If no normalization method is selected, the quality-controlled dataset is retained without additional normalization.






ImportantApplying normalization



Selecting a normalization method does not immediately modify the dataset.
After selecting the desired methods, click Apply selected normalization to apply the transformations and update the dataset used by the downstream analysis modules.

title: Normalization
text:
log2 transformation
The log2 transformation converts quantitative intensity measurements to the log2 scale.
This transformation compresses the range of protein intensities and can reduce the influence of very large abundance measurements.
Non-finite values generated during transformation are replaced with zero.






NoteZero values



Because log2(0) is not finite, zero-valued measurements remain represented as zero after the transformation rather than as negative infinity.

title: Normalization
text:
Within replicate median normalization
The Within replicate median normalization option adjusts measurements according to the median abundance observed for each temperature and replicate.
For each temperature, TPP Analyst calculates the overall median abundance across finite, non-zero measurements. The median for each replicate at the same temperature is then compared with this overall value.
The difference between the replicate-specific median and the overall median is used to adjust the corresponding measurements.
Zero values remain zero during this normalization.
This procedure can reduce systematic abundance differences between replicates while maintaining the temperature-dependent structure of the dataset.

title: Normalization
text:
Normalize to lowest temperature
The Normalize to lowest temperature option expresses the thermal profile of each protein relative to its abundance at the lowest measured temperature.
Normalization is performed independently for each replicate.
For each protein and replicate:

The lowest experimental temperature is identified.
The abundance measured at that temperature is used as the reference value.
All temperature points within the same replicate are divided by this reference value.

Consequently, the lowest-temperature measurement becomes the reference point for each thermal profile.
For example, if a replicate contains measurements at:
40°C
43°C
46°C
49°C
52°C
the abundance at 40°C is used as the denominator for the measurements belonging to that replicate.






ImportantInvalid reference measurements



If the lowest-temperature reference measurement for a protein is zero or missing, the corresponding normalized measurements for that replicate cannot be calculated and are returned as missing values.








TipThermal profile normalization



Normalization to the lowest temperature is particularly useful when the downstream analysis focuses on relative changes in protein abundance across the thermal gradient rather than differences in absolute protein abundance.

title: Normalization
text:
Reference protein normalization
The Reference protein normalization option expresses quantitative measurements relative to a selected reference protein.
Two approaches are available:

Manually select
Program estimation


Manual reference protein selection
Select Manually select and enter the protein accession to use as the reference.
TPP Analyst searches for the specified accession in the current dataset.
For every quantitative measurement, protein abundances are divided by the corresponding abundance of the selected reference protein.
If the specified accession cannot be found, TPP Analyst reports that the reference protein is not present in the dataset.






WarningReference protein selection



The manually entered protein identifier must correspond to an accession present in the current dataset.




Automatic reference protein estimation
Select Program estimation to allow TPP Analyst to identify a reference protein automatically.
The application calculates the standard deviation of each protein profile across the quantitative measurements and selects the protein with the lowest standard deviation as the reference.
This selects the protein displaying the most stable quantitative profile according to this criterion.


Reference protein information
After reference protein normalization has been applied, TPP Analyst displays the accession of the reference protein used.
When the corresponding organism annotation is available, the application can additionally display:

the protein name;
the gene name.







NoteReference protein removal



The reference protein itself is removed from the normalized dataset after reference protein normalization has been applied.

title: Normalization
text:
Combining normalization methods
Multiple normalization methods can be selected simultaneously.
When multiple methods are selected, TPP Analyst applies the selected transformations sequentially.
According to the current workflow, selected methods are evaluated in the following order:

log2 transformation
Within replicate median normalization
Normalize to lowest temperature
Reference protein normalization







ImportantOrder of transformations



When combining normalization methods, the transformations are not independent. Each selected method operates on the dataset produced by the preceding normalization step.
The order of the selected transformations should therefore be considered when configuring the analysis.

title: Normalization
text:
Intensity distribution across samples
The Intensity distribution across samples plot provides a sample-level overview of the quantitative values after the current normalization settings have been applied.
Each boxplot represents one temperature-replicate combination.
Samples are shown along the X-axis, while the Y-axis represents the corresponding protein intensity or transformed intensity.
The sample boxes are colored according to temperature.






Figure 2: Intensity distribution across samples.



This plot can be used to inspect whether systematic differences remain between temperatures or replicates after normalization.

Including zero values
By default, zero values are excluded from the intensity distribution plot.
Enable:
Include zero values in the plot
to include zero-valued measurements in the displayed distributions.






TipEvaluating normalization



Compare the distributions across samples after normalization. Large systematic differences between comparable samples may indicate that additional inspection of the data or normalization strategy is required.

title: Normalization
text:
Global intensity distribution
The Global intensity distribution plot compares individual protein thermal profiles with the overall average profile of the dataset.
Each colored line represents the mean thermal profile of an individual protein across replicates.
The thick black line represents the average abundance profile across all proteins.

Distance from the global profile
For each protein, TPP Analyst calculates its distance from the global average thermal profile across the measured temperatures.
The distance is based on the squared differences between the individual protein profile and the global average profile.
Protein lines are visually weighted according to their similarity to the global profile.
Proteins that closely follow the overall thermal trend are visually emphasized, while proteins showing profiles that differ more strongly from the global trend are displayed less prominently.






Figure 3: Global intensity distribution.



This visualization can help distinguish the dominant thermal response of the dataset from proteins displaying atypical abundance profiles.


Including zero values
By default, zero measurements are excluded when calculating the protein-level mean profiles used in this visualization.
Enable:
Include zero values in mean calculation
to include zero measurements when calculating the displayed protein trends.






NoteZero-value handling



The zero-value controls for the intensity distribution boxplot and the global intensity distribution are independent.
Changing these display options does not itself alter the underlying normalized dataset.

title: Normalization
text:
Sample clustering and outlier detection
TPP Analyst uses Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to examine similarities between samples and identify measurements that may behave differently from the rest of the experiment.
Two PCA modes are available:

By sample
By condition

The percentage of variance explained by PC1 and PC2 is displayed directly in the corresponding axis labels.

title: Normalization
text:
PCA by sample
The By sample mode performs PCA on the current dataset.






Figure 4: PCA by sample.



Each point represents a temperature-replicate sample.
Points are:

colored according to temperature;
associated with replicate information.

Hovering over a point displays the corresponding replicate and temperature.
The PCA can be used to assess whether samples with similar experimental characteristics occupy similar regions of the reduced-dimensional space and to identify potential sample-level outliers.






TipPCA interpretation



Samples positioned far from otherwise comparable samples may warrant further inspection. Potential outliers should be evaluated in the context of the experimental design and the other QC diagnostics before being removed.

title: Normalization
text:
PCA by condition
The By condition mode compares samples across multiple experimental datasets.






Figure 5: PCA by condition.



Each point represents a sample associated with an experimental condition, temperature, and replicate.
Points are colored according to condition.
This view can be used to investigate the relationships between experimental conditions and determine whether condition-associated structure contributes to the major sources of variation in the dataset.






NoteMultiple datasets required



The By condition PCA requires more than one dataset to perform the comparison.

title: Normalization
text:
Variance decomposition
Enable:
Show variance decomposition
to replace the standard PCA visualization with a summary of the sources of variance associated with the principal components.
For PCA by sample, the visualization separates the variance into:

Batch variance, based on replicate;
Residual variance.

For PCA by condition, the visualization separates variance into:

Batch variance, based on replicate;
Condition variance;
Residual variance.

The variance decomposition is shown for up to the first 10 principal components.
This visualization can help determine whether major components of variation are associated with replicate structure, experimental condition, or other unexplained variation.

title: Normalization
text:
Selecting samples from the PCA
The PCA visualization is interactive.
Click a sample directly in the PCA plot to add it to the Samples to remove table.
Selected samples remain in this table until they are removed or the selection is changed.
Click:
Remove selected
to exclude selected samples from the working dataset.
Removed samples are displayed in the Removed samples table.






WarningRemoving samples



Removing a sample changes the quantitative dataset used for normalization and downstream analyses.
Sample removal should therefore be based on the experimental design and supporting evidence rather than PCA position alone.

title: Normalization
text:
Restoring removed samples
Samples that have been removed are retained in the Removed samples table.
Select the desired sample and click:
Restore selected
to return the sample to the analysis.
This allows sample removal decisions to be reversed without restarting the complete analysis workflow.

title: Normalization
section: Reapplying normalization after removing or restoring samples
text:
Reapplying normalization after removing or restoring samples
Whenever samples are removed or restored, the previously calculated normalization is no longer considered current.
TPP Analyst displays a warning:
Samples were removed or restored in the PCA section.
Please click 'Apply selected normalization' again to recompute all normalization steps.
After changing the sample set, click Apply selected normalization again.
This recalculates the normalization using the updated dataset.






ImportantReapply normalization after changing samples



Always click Apply selected normalization after removing or restoring samples.
This ensures that the normalization and downstream analyses are based on the current set of samples.

title: Normalization
text:
Coefficient of variation
The Coefficient of variation plot summarizes variability between replicates at each temperature.






Figure 6: Coefficient of variation plot.



For each protein and temperature, the coefficient of variation is calculated from the available replicate measurements.
Zero measurements are excluded from the CV calculation.
At least two non-zero replicate measurements are required for a protein to contribute a CV value at a particular temperature.
For data on the standard abundance scale, the coefficient of variation is calculated from the standard deviation relative to the mean abundance.
The resulting CV distributions are displayed as boxplots for each temperature.

Interpreting CV values
Lower CV values indicate closer agreement between replicate measurements, while higher values indicate greater replicate-to-replicate variability.
Comparing distributions across temperatures can help identify regions of the thermal gradient associated with increased experimental variability.






TipReplicate consistency



Use the CV plot together with PCA and the sample intensity distributions. A sample or temperature displaying unusual behavior across several complementary diagnostics may warrant closer inspection.

title: Normalization
text:
Recommended normalization workflow
A typical normalization workflow in TPP Analyst is:

Review the quality-controlled dataset.
Select the desired normalization method or combination of methods.
Configure the reference protein if reference normalization is selected.
Click Apply selected normalization.
Inspect the intensity distributions across samples.
Inspect the global intensity distribution.
Examine PCA by sample.
Inspect the variance decomposition when useful.
Use PCA by condition when comparing multiple datasets.
Inspect the coefficient of variation across temperatures.
Investigate potential problematic samples using the available diagnostics.
Remove a sample only when supported by the experimental context and QC evidence.
Reapply normalization if samples are removed or restored.
Reassess the diagnostic plots after normalization has been recalculated.
Proceed to clustering when the normalized dataset is satisfactory.







ImportantNormalized data are used downstream



The current normalized dataset is passed to subsequent TPP Analyst modules. Normalization settings and sample-removal decisions can therefore affect clustering, model fitting, protein-level visualization, and downstream statistical analyses.

title: Normalization
text:
Next step
Once normalization has been applied and the diagnostic visualizations have been reviewed, continue to Clustering.

title: Input Data
text:
TPP Analyst requires quantitative protein abundance data together with an experimental design describing the structure of the experiment.
TPP Analyst supports the following file formats:

title: Input Data
text:
Experimental design
The experimental design describes how the quantitative measurements are associated with the experiment.
The required columns are:

File Name
Condition
Temperature
Replicate







Figure 1: Example structure of an experimental design.




File Name
The File Name column identifies the quantitative measurement corresponding to the protein abundance dataset.


Condition
The Condition column identifies the experimental condition associated with each measurement.
Examples include:

Control
Vehicle
Treatment



Temperature
The Temperature column contains the experimental temperature associated with each measurement.
Temperature values must be numeric.


Replicate
The Replicate column identifies the replicate associated with each measurement.
Each combination of condition, temperature, and replicate should correspond to the appropriate quantitative measurement in the protein abundance dataset.

title: Input Data
text:
Protein abundance dataset
The protein abundance dataset contains the protein identifiers and quantitative measurements.
The required identifier column is:
Accession
Each row represents a protein, while the remaining quantitative columns contain the protein abundance measurements associated with the experiment linked to the values of the Experimental Design column: File Name.






Figure 2: Example structure of a protein abundance dataset.




Protein identifiers
Each value in the Accession column must be unique.






TipRecommendation



UniProt accession identifiers are recommended, particularly when GO analysis will be performed.








WarningDuplicate identifiers



The Accession column must contain unique identifiers. Duplicated protein identifiers must be resolved before the dataset can be processed.




Organism column
For experiments containing multiple organisms, the protein abundance dataset must additionally contain an Organism column.
For single-organism experiments, this column is optional.
All remaining columns should contain the quantitative protein abundance measurements corresponding to the samples described in the experimental design.

title: Input Data
text:
Organism selection
TPP Analyst supports both single-organism and multi-organism experiments.

Single-organism experiments
When a single organism is selected, the Organism column in the protein abundance dataset is optional.
The selected organism is associated with the processed datasets automatically.


Multi-organism experiments
When multiple organisms are selected, the protein abundance dataset must contain an additional column named:
Organism
Each protein must be associated with its corresponding organism.






ImportantMulti-organism datasets



The Organism column is required when more than one organism is present in the experiment.


TPP Analyst can recognize supported organism names when they occur within longer organism descriptions.
For example:
Sulfolobus acidocaldarius DSM 639
can be recognized as:
Sulfolobus acidocaldarius
This allows organism entries containing additional information, such as strain information, to be associated with the corresponding supported organism.

title: Input Data
text:
Condition-to-organism mapping
For multi-organism experiments, TPP Analyst requires the organisms present in each experimental condition to be specified.
Assign the appropriate organism or organisms to each experimental condition before loading the protein abundance dataset.






Figure 3: Condition-to-organism mapping for a multi-organism experiment.



The condition-to-organism mapping is subsequently used when the processed datasets are separated according to condition and organism.

title: Input Data
text:
Other organisms
If the organism being analyzed is not included among the predefined organisms, select Other.
The Other option allows custom organisms to be incorporated into the analysis workflow.
Additional organism-specific information can subsequently be provided when required for organism-dependent analyses such as Gene Ontology analysis.






Figure 4: Other organisms and custom GO terms dataset loading.









NoteCustom organisms



Use the Other option when the organism is not available among the predefined selections. Ensure that the organism information in the protein dataset correctly identifies the proteins belonging to the custom organism.

title: Input Data
text:
Custom organism GO database
TPP Analyst includes built-in annotation databases for the predefined organisms available in the organism selector.
When an organism is not included in the predefined list, select:
Other
and provide a name for the custom organism.
A custom organism annotation file can then be uploaded to provide the protein and Gene Ontology information required for downstream functional enrichment analysis.






NoteWhen is a custom GO database needed?



The custom organism database is not required for the general processing, quality control, normalization, clustering, model fitting, or comparison of TPP datasets.
However, a compatible annotation database should be provided when GO enrichment analysis will be performed for an organism selected as Other.



Obtaining a custom organism database
Custom organism annotation files can be downloaded from UniProt for the organism of interest.






Figure 5: Custom organism GO database structure.



The downloaded file should contain protein identifiers together with protein, gene, organism, and Gene Ontology annotations.
TPP Analyst supports custom organism databases in the following formats:

CSV (.csv)
TSV (.tsv)
text (.txt)
Excel (.xlsx)
Excel (.xls)



Required columns
The custom organism database must contain the following columns:
Entry
Protein names
Gene Names
Organism
Gene Ontology (GO)
Gene Ontology (biological process)
Gene Ontology (cellular component)
Gene Ontology (molecular function)
Gene Ontology IDs






ImportantKeep the UniProt column names unchanged



The required column names should be retained exactly as provided by UniProt.
If required columns are missing, TPP Analyst will report the custom organism database as invalid and identify the missing columns.




Protein identifiers
The Entry column contains the protein identifiers used to associate the custom annotation database with proteins in the experimental dataset.
For the most reliable matching, the identifiers in the Accession column of the protein abundance dataset should correspond to the UniProt identifiers provided in the Entry column of the custom organism database.






TipRecommendation



When using a custom organism database, use UniProt accession identifiers in the protein abundance dataset whenever possible.
Consistent identifiers between the protein dataset and the custom annotation database improve the matching of proteins to GO annotations.




GO annotation columns
The custom database provides several complementary Gene Ontology annotation fields.
The following columns provide annotations for the three major GO categories:
Gene Ontology (biological process)
Gene Ontology (cellular component)
Gene Ontology (molecular function)
These correspond to:

Biological Process (BP)
Cellular Component (CC)
Molecular Function (MF)

The:
Gene Ontology IDs
column provides the corresponding GO identifiers.
These annotations are subsequently used by TPP Analyst to construct the protein-to-GO mappings required for ORA and GSEA.


Custom organism name
For a single-organism experiment, selecting Other displays a field where the custom organism name can be entered.
For example:
My custom organism
The custom database uploaded for the experiment is associated with this organism name.
For multi-organism experiments, custom organism names are specified separately for the experimental conditions in which Other was selected.


Custom databases in multi-organism experiments
A custom organism can also be combined with predefined organisms in a multi-organism experiment.
For example, a condition could contain:
Homo sapiens
Other
The predefined human annotation database is used for Homo sapiens, while the uploaded custom annotation database provides the annotation information for the organism represented by Other.
When Other is assigned to a condition, enter the corresponding custom organism name and upload its organism database.






TipMixed-proteome experiments



The custom organism functionality allows TPP Analyst to analyze mixed-proteome experiments containing both predefined and user-provided organisms.
The Organism column in the protein abundance dataset should clearly identify which proteins belong to each organism.




Organism names in the uploaded database
After a custom organism database is loaded, TPP Analyst associates the uploaded annotations with the custom organism name provided in the interface.
This allows the custom organism name used throughout the analysis to remain consistent even when the original UniProt organism annotation contains additional naming information.


Validation
TPP Analyst validates the structure of the custom organism database when it is uploaded.
If required columns are missing, an error message identifies the missing fields and the annotation database cannot be used until the required structure is provided.






WarningCustom database validation



Before continuing, ensure that the custom annotation file contains all required UniProt annotation columns.
An incomplete database may prevent GO annotation matching and downstream enrichment analysis.




Relationship between the three input files
When a custom organism is used, the input workflow can therefore contain three types of files:
Experimental design
        +
Protein abundance dataset
        +
Custom organism GO database
Their roles are different:

The experimental design describes conditions, temperatures, and replicates.
The protein abundance dataset provides the quantitative protein measurements.
The custom organism GO database provides organism-specific protein and functional annotations for downstream GO analysis.

The custom GO database does not replace either of the two primary experimental input files.

title: Input Data
text:
Example datasets
TPP Analyst includes the Staurosporine thermal proteome profiling dataset from the landmark study by Savitski et al. (Science, 2014) - DOI: 10.1126/science.1255784 as example datasets that can be loaded directly from the application.
The example dataset allow the analysis workflow to be explored without uploading custom files and provide examples of data structures compatible with TPP Analyst.

title: Input Data
text:
Dataset splitting
After the input files have been validated, TPP Analyst organizes the protein abundance measurements according to the experimental design.
The available splitting options depend on the number of organisms represented in the experiment.

Condition only
The Condition only option generates one analysis dataset for each experimental condition.
For example:
Vehicle
Treatment
All proteins associated with an experimental condition remain within the same dataset.


Condition + Organism
For multi-organism experiments, the Condition + Organism option additionally separates proteins according to organism.
For example:
Human_Homo sapiens
Mixed_Homo sapiens
Mixed_Sulfolobus acidocaldarius
Sulfolobus_Sulfolobus acidocaldarius
This allows proteins belonging to different organisms within the same experimental condition to be analyzed independently.






Figure 6: Selecting how the processed datasets should be split.









TipChoosing a splitting strategy



Use Condition only when all proteins within an experimental condition should remain together.
Use Condition + Organism when proteins from different organisms within the same experimental condition should be analyzed independently.

title: Input Data
Clustering
text:
The Clustering module groups proteins according to similarities in their thermal abundance profiles across the temperature gradient.
Clustering can be performed on an individual experimental condition or across multiple conditions. TPP Analyst also provides silhouette-based guidance for selecting the number of clusters and allows individual clusters to be further divided using sub-clustering.
The main steps of the clustering workflow are:

title: Clustering
text:
Clustering controls






Figure 1: Clustering controls.



Clustering is based on similarities between protein thermal profiles.
TPP Analyst calculates the correlation between protein profiles and uses the resulting correlation-based dissimilarities to perform hierarchical clustering.
Two clustering modes are available:

Individual condition
Condition comparison

title: Clustering
text:
Individual condition
The Individual condition mode performs clustering using the thermal profiles from the current dataset.
Each protein is represented by its measurements across temperatures and replicates.
Proteins displaying similar thermal abundance patterns are grouped into the same cluster.
This mode is useful for exploring the major thermal-profile patterns present within a single experimental condition.

title: Clustering
text:
Condition comparison
The Condition comparison mode allows protein profiles from multiple datasets to be considered simultaneously.
Select the datasets to include using:
Select datasets for comparison
The measurements belonging to the same protein across the selected datasets are combined into a single profile before the correlation between proteins is calculated.
This allows proteins to be clustered according to their collective behavior across multiple experimental conditions.






TipIndividual versus comparison clustering



Use Individual condition to identify groups of proteins with similar thermal profiles within one dataset.
Use Condition comparison when you want clustering to consider how proteins behave across several experimental conditions simultaneously.



Combining proteins across datasets
In comparison mode, datasets are matched using the protein accession.
The quantitative measurements from the selected datasets are then combined before clustering.
This allows the clustering result to reflect protein behavior across all included datasets rather than evaluating the datasets independently.






NoteProtein identifiers



Comparison clustering relies on the protein accession to associate protein measurements between datasets. Consistent protein identifiers are therefore important when comparing conditions.

title: Clustering
text:
Correlation method
TPP Analyst provides two correlation methods:

Pearson
Spearman

The selected correlation method determines how similarity between protein thermal profiles is calculated.

Pearson correlation
Pearson correlation measures the linear relationship between two protein profiles.
Proteins with similar quantitative patterns across the thermal gradient will have stronger positive correlations.


Spearman correlation
Spearman correlation compares the ranked values of the protein profiles.
Because it is based on ranks, Spearman correlation focuses more strongly on the overall ordering and shape of the abundance profiles rather than requiring a linear relationship between their absolute values.
Spearman correlation is selected by default in TPP Analyst.






TipChoosing a correlation method



Use Pearson when similarity in the quantitative shape and magnitude of the profiles is important.
Use Spearman when the relative pattern across temperatures is more important and you want the clustering to be less dependent on the exact quantitative relationship between profiles.

title: Clustering
text:
Number of clusters
The Select number of clusters (k) control specifies how many groups will be generated.
TPP Analyst allows values between:
2 and 10
The default value is:
k = 4
After selecting the desired number of clusters and correlation method, click:
Run clustering
The selected number of clusters is used to divide the hierarchical clustering tree into the requested groups.






NoteChoosing k



The manually selected value of k determines the clustering result.
TPP Analyst also calculates a silhouette-based recommendation after clustering has been run to help evaluate whether another value of k may provide better separation.

title: Clustering
text:
Cluster recommendation
After clustering has been performed, TPP Analyst evaluates alternative numbers of clusters using silhouette analysis.






Figure 2: Silhouette analysis plot.



The silhouette score measures how well each protein matches its assigned cluster relative to neighboring clusters.
Higher average silhouette scores indicate stronger separation between the resulting clusters.
TPP Analyst evaluates candidate values of k from 2 up to a maximum of 10, depending on the number of proteins available in the dataset.
The application reports:

the recommended number of clusters;
the corresponding average silhouette score.

title: Clustering
text:
Cluster quality assessment plot
The cluster quality assessment plot displays the average silhouette score as a function of the number of clusters.
The X-axis represents:
Number of clusters (k)
and the Y-axis represents:
Average silhouette score
The recommended value of k is indicated by a red dashed line.






ImportantRecommendation versus selected k



The silhouette result is a recommendation and does not automatically replace the value of k selected by the user.
If the recommended value differs from the current clustering solution, change the number of clusters and click Run clustering again to generate the corresponding result.








TipUsing the silhouette recommendation



The highest silhouette score provides a useful statistical criterion for selecting k, but clustering should also be evaluated biologically.
Inspect the resulting thermal-profile trends, cluster sizes, and heatmap before deciding which clustering solution is most informative for the experiment.

title: Clustering
Clustering
text:
Individual protein trends
Individual protein profiles are displayed as thin lines.
For each protein, replicate measurements are summarized at each temperature to generate its thermal abundance profile.
These individual profiles provide an overview of the variability among proteins assigned to the same cluster.

title: Clustering
text:
Average cluster trend
A stronger line represents the average thermal profile of all proteins assigned to the corresponding cluster.
The average trend provides a concise representation of the dominant thermal behavior of each group.
The number of proteins assigned to each cluster is displayed as:
n = number of proteins
This allows both the shape and size of each cluster to be assessed.

title: Clustering
section: Missing and zero values in trend plots
text:
Missing and zero values in trend plots
The cluster visualization provides the option:
Show missing values as zero
When this option is disabled, zero-valued measurements are omitted from the calculation of the displayed thermal trends.
When the option is enabled, zero measurements are retained in the visualization.






ImportantVisualization versus clustering



The Show missing values as zero setting controls how zero values are represented in the cluster trend visualization.
Changing this checkbox does not rerun the clustering or alter the existing cluster assignments.

title: Clustering
text:
Custom Y-axis range
Enable:
Set custom Y-axis range
to manually control the displayed Y-axis of the cluster trend plots.
Two values can then be specified:

Y-axis minimum
Y-axis maximum

This can be useful when a small number of proteins have unusually large abundance values that expand the plot range and make the dominant cluster trends difficult to inspect.






TipAdjusting the Y-axis



Changing the Y-axis range affects only the displayed portion of the cluster trend plot.
It does not remove proteins, modify their abundance values, or recalculate the clustering result.

title: Clustering
text:
Condition comparison visualization
When clustering is performed using Condition comparison, each cluster shows the profiles of the datasets included in the comparison.






Figure 4: Clustered data for condition comparison mode.



Individual protein profiles are displayed together with stronger average profiles representing the general thermal trend for each dataset.
The dataset-specific trends are distinguished using color.
This visualization can be used to investigate whether proteins assigned to the same cluster show similar or contrasting behavior between experimental conditions.

title: Clustering
text:
Cluster heatmap
TPP Analyst generates a heatmap containing the proteins used in the clustering analysis.






Figure 5: Clustered data heatmap.



Each row represents a protein and each column represents a quantitative measurement.
Protein abundance is represented by the heatmap color scale.
Proteins are organized according to their assigned cluster and the hierarchical clustering structure.
A cluster annotation identifies the cluster associated with each protein.






NoteConsistent cluster colors



Cluster colors are shared between the cluster trend visualization and the cluster heatmap.
The same color therefore identifies the same cluster across the two visualizations.



Heatmap organization
Measurement columns are arranged according to:

dataset;
temperature;
replicate.

In comparison mode, dataset names are displayed above their corresponding groups of measurements.
This organization makes it easier to compare thermal patterns between temperatures, replicates, and experimental datasets.

title: Clustering
text:
Sub-clustering
TPP Analyst allows an existing cluster to be subjected to a second clustering analysis.
This functionality can be useful when a broad cluster contains several more specific thermal response patterns that are not resolved in the initial clustering result.
Expand the:
Sub-cluster data
section to access the sub-clustering controls.

title: Clustering
text:
Selecting a cluster to sub-cluster
Use:
Select cluster to sub-cluster (1 to k)
to specify which cluster from the original clustering result should be analyzed further.
Only the proteins assigned to the selected cluster are included in the sub-clustering analysis.

title: Clustering
text:
Number of sub-clusters
Use:
Select number of clusters for sub-clustering
to specify how many new groups should be generated within the selected original cluster.
The available range is:
2 to 10
The selected original cluster must contain enough proteins to support the requested number of sub-clusters.
Click:
Run Sub-clustering
to generate the new clustering solution.

title: Clustering
text:
Sub-cluster recommendation
TPP Analyst also performs silhouette analysis within the selected original cluster.
The procedure evaluates alternative values for the number of sub-clusters and identifies the value associated with the highest average silhouette score.
For the recommendation to be calculated, the selected original cluster must contain at least five proteins.
The application reports:

the recommended number of sub-clusters;
the corresponding average silhouette score.

A sub-cluster quality assessment plot displays the silhouette scores across the candidate values of k.






NoteSub-cluster recommendation



Sub-cluster silhouette analysis is performed only on the proteins belonging to the selected original cluster.
The recommendation may therefore differ substantially from the optimal number of clusters for the complete dataset.

title: Clustering
Clustering
section: Missing and zero values in sub-cluster plots
text:
Missing and zero values in sub-cluster plots
The sub-cluster visualization has its own independent control:
Show missing values as zero (sub-clustering plot)
When disabled, zero-valued measurements are omitted from the displayed trends.
When enabled, zero measurements are retained in the visualization.
This control affects the sub-cluster trend display independently of the corresponding setting in the main clustering plot.

title: Clustering
text:
Custom Y-axis range for sub-clusters
The sub-cluster visualization also provides:
Set custom Y-axis range
When enabled, specify:

Y-axis minimum
Y-axis maximum

This allows the displayed abundance range to be adjusted independently for the sub-cluster visualization.






NoteIndependent visualization settings



The main clustering and sub-clustering trend plots have separate controls for zero-value display and Y-axis limits.
Changing the settings of one visualization does not modify the corresponding settings of the other.

title: Clustering
text:
Sub-cluster heatmap
TPP Analyst generates a heatmap containing only proteins belonging to the selected original cluster.
Proteins are ordered according to their new sub-cluster assignments and hierarchical clustering structure.
A colored annotation identifies the sub-cluster assigned to each protein.
For comparison analyses, samples remain organized by dataset, temperature, and replicate.






NoteConsistent sub-cluster colors



Sub-cluster colors are shared between the sub-cluster trend plot and the sub-cluster heatmap.
A given color therefore represents the same sub-cluster across both visualizations.

title: Clustering
text:
Recommended clustering workflow
A typical clustering analysis in TPP Analyst is:

Decide whether the analysis should use an individual condition or compare multiple conditions.
Select the datasets when using condition comparison.
Select Pearson or Spearman correlation.
Choose an initial number of clusters.
Click Run clustering.
Inspect the silhouette recommendation and cluster quality plot.
If appropriate, change k and rerun the clustering.
Inspect the individual protein profiles and average trend within each cluster.
Check the number of proteins assigned to each cluster.
Adjust the zero-value display if needed.
Adjust the Y-axis range if extreme values obscure the main trends.
Inspect the cluster heatmap.
Identify clusters containing potentially distinct internal thermal patterns.
Select an original cluster for sub-clustering when additional resolution is required.
Inspect the sub-cluster silhouette recommendation.
Select the desired number of sub-clusters and run the analysis.
Inspect the sub-cluster trends and heatmap.
Export the relevant visualizations.







ImportantInterpret clusters as patterns



Clustering is an exploratory analysis. Cluster assignments identify groups of proteins with similar quantitative thermal profiles under the selected clustering settings.
The resulting groups should be interpreted together with the experimental design, cluster sizes, thermal trends, and downstream biological analyses.

title: Clustering
text:
Next step
After identifying and examining the major thermal-profile patterns in the dataset, continue to Model Fitting.

title: Comparison Models
text:
The Comparison Models section provides statistical approaches for identifying proteins whose thermal stability differs between experimental conditions.
TPP Analyst provides two complementary comparison methods:
The TPP approach is centered on melting-temperature shifts, whereas NPARC evaluates differences across the complete thermal profile and can therefore identify changes that are not necessarily characterized by a large shift in Tm.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Selecting conditions
Select the two datasets to compare using:

Vehicle condition
Treatment condition

Although these controls are labelled Vehicle and Treatment, they represent the two experimental datasets that will be compared.






Figure 1: TPP control panel



The selected datasets should correspond to biologically meaningful comparison groups.
For example:
Vehicle
Treatment
or:
Control
Drug

title: Comparison Models
text:
Replicate comparisons
TPP Analyst identifies the replicate structure of the selected datasets and creates corresponding comparisons between the two conditions.
For example:
Vehicle replicate 1
        vs
Treatment replicate 1

Vehicle replicate 2
        vs
Treatment replicate 2
Melting curves are fitted for each protein within these replicate comparisons.
The resulting Tm differences and statistical results are subsequently combined in the TPP output.






NoteReplicate structure



TPP comparison assumes corresponding replicate structures between the two selected datasets.
Review the experimental design before running the analysis to ensure that the replicate assignments accurately represent the intended comparison.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Minimum R²
The:
Minimum R²
control defines the minimum accepted curve-fit quality.
The default value is:
0.8
Increasing the threshold applies a more stringent curve-quality criterion.
Proteins with fitted curves below the selected R² threshold do not pass the corresponding replicate filter.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Maximum Plateau
The:
Maximum Plateau
control specifies the highest accepted fitted plateau value.
The default value is:
0.3
Proteins whose fitted curves exceed this plateau threshold do not pass the corresponding replicate quality filter.






TipCurve-quality filtering



R² and plateau thresholds should be chosen to retain reliable thermal profiles while avoiding overly stringent filtering that removes large portions of the dataset.
Use the result summary and individual protein curves to assess the effect of the selected thresholds.

title: Comparison Models
Comparison Models
text:
Mean ΔTm
Mean_DeltaTm represents the average melting-temperature difference across the available replicate comparisons for a protein.
A positive ΔTm indicates that the estimated melting temperature is higher in the treatment condition relative to the vehicle condition.
A negative ΔTm indicates that the estimated melting temperature is lower in the treatment condition.






NoteInterpreting ΔTm



ΔTm describes the direction and magnitude of the estimated thermal stability shift.
The statistical significance, replicate consistency, and curve quality should also be considered when interpreting an individual protein.

title: Comparison Models
text:
SD of ΔTm
SD_DeltaTm summarizes the variability of the ΔTm estimates across replicate comparisons.
Lower variability indicates greater agreement between replicate-specific thermal shifts.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Minimum adjusted p-value
Min_Adjusted_P reports the smallest adjusted p-value observed across the available replicate comparisons for the protein.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Replicates passing
Replicates_Passing reports how many replicate comparisons satisfy the selected TPP curve-quality criteria.
This provides a direct indication of the replicate support available for the reported protein result.

title: Comparison Models
section: Show only proteins passing all replicate comparisons
text:
Show only proteins passing all replicate comparisons
Enable:
Show only proteins passing all replicate comparisons
to restrict the results to proteins that pass the selected curve-quality filters in every replicate comparison.
This provides a more stringent result set supported by all available replicate comparisons.

title: Comparison Models
section: Show only proteins with ΔTm calculated
text:
Show only proteins with ΔTm calculated
Enable:
Show only proteins with ΔTm calculated in at least one replicate
to restrict the displayed table to proteins for which a finite ΔTm result is available in at least one replicate comparison.






TipFiltering TPP results



Use these options to move between a broad overview of the analysis and a more stringent set of proteins with stronger replicate and curve-quality support.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Adjusted p-value distribution
The Adjusted p-value distribution histogram displays the adjusted p-values generated across replicate comparisons.
This provides a global view of the statistical significance landscape of the TPP analysis.
An accumulation of small adjusted p-values indicates a larger number of proteins with statistical evidence for thermal stability differences.

title: Comparison Models
text:
ΔTm distribution
The Delta Tm distribution histogram summarizes the melting-temperature differences observed across the replicate comparisons.
The distribution provides an overview of:

the direction of thermal shifts;
their overall magnitude;
the presence of proteins with unusually large positive or negative ΔTm values.







NoteGlobal distributions



The adjusted p-value and ΔTm distributions are diagnostic summaries of the complete analysis.
Protein-level conclusions should be based on the individual statistical results together with replicate support and inspection of the corresponding melting curves.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Empirical method
The empirical option uses the empirical NPARC approach for determining the F-test statistics and corresponding significance estimates.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Theoretical method
The theoretical option uses the theoretical F-distribution-based approach.






TipComparing F-statistic methods



Because both methods are calculated during the same model-comparison run, the selector can be used to inspect how the resulting statistical evidence changes between the empirical and theoretical approaches.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Minimum RSS difference
The:
Minimum RSS difference
control allows the result table to be further restricted according to the magnitude of model-fit improvement.
The default value is:
0
Increasing this threshold restricts the table to proteins showing progressively larger improvements when condition-specific models are fitted.






TipCombining statistical significance and model improvement



The adjusted p-value and RSS-difference filters provide complementary criteria.
The adjusted p-value reflects statistical evidence, while the RSS difference reflects the magnitude by which the alternative model improves the fit relative to the null model.

title: Comparison Models
text:
rss_null
rss_null is the residual sum of squares obtained from the shared null model.

title: Comparison Models
text:
rss_alt
rss_alt represents the residual sum of squares obtained from the condition-specific alternative model or models.

title: Comparison Models
text:
rss_diff
rss_diff is calculated as:
rss_null - rss_alt
Larger positive values indicate a greater reduction in residual error when separate condition-specific curves are used.

title: Comparison Models
text:
F statistic
fStat describes the improvement in model fit relative to the additional flexibility introduced by the alternative model.
Larger F statistics indicate stronger evidence that the condition-specific model provides a better description of the protein thermal profiles.

title: Comparison Models
text:
P-value
pVal reports the statistical significance associated with the F-test.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Adjusted p-value
pAdj reports the p-value after correction for multiple testing.
This value is used by the adjusted p-value filter in the interface.

title: Comparison Models
text:
P-value distribution
The P-value distribution histogram displays the unadjusted p-values produced by the selected NPARC F-test method.
This provides an overview of the statistical significance landscape across the tested proteins.

title: Comparison Models
text:
F statistic distribution
The F statistic distribution displays the observed F statistics.
To prevent extreme F statistics from dominating the visualization, the displayed X-axis is restricted to the 99th percentile of the finite F-statistic distribution.
This makes the main body of the distribution easier to inspect.

title: Comparison Models
text:
Observed versus expected F distribution
The F distribution fit compares the observed F-statistic density with the corresponding theoretical F distribution.
The observed distribution is displayed as a density curve, while the theoretical expectation is shown as a red line.
The theoretical curve is generated using representative degrees of freedom from the current results.
The plot title indicates whether the empirical or theoretical NPARC method is currently selected.






TipF-distribution diagnostic



Use this plot to inspect how the observed test statistics compare with the expected theoretical distribution.
This diagnostic can help identify deviations in the overall F-statistic distribution that may be relevant when interpreting the model-comparison results.

title: Comparison Models
text:
RSS difference distribution
The RSS difference distribution displays:
RSSnull - RSSalt
across the tested proteins.
Positive values indicate that the condition-specific alternative model decreases residual error relative to the shared null model.
Proteins with larger positive RSS differences show greater improvements in fit under the alternative model.

title: Model Fitting
text:
The Model Fitting module provides complementary approaches for investigating temperature-dependent protein abundance profiles.
Two analyses are available:
These approaches provide different perspectives on protein thermal behavior and can be used independently depending on the objectives of the analysis.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Selecting the null hypothesis
The Select the Null hypothesis to test control determines the type of thermal behavior evaluated by the analysis.






Figure 1: Null hypothesis selection.




Slope significantly different from zero
Select:
Is the slope of the proteins significantly different from 0?
to identify proteins whose abundance changes significantly with temperature.
Under this model, temperature is used to estimate the direction and magnitude of the abundance trend for each protein.
Proteins with statistically significant slopes display evidence of systematic changes in abundance across the thermal gradient.


Slope significantly different from the average trend
Select:
Is the slope of the proteins significantly different from the average trend?
to identify proteins whose thermal behavior differs from the overall proteome-wide response.
Before statistical testing, the average abundance profile across proteins is calculated and removed from the individual protein measurements.
The analysis therefore focuses on proteins whose temperature-dependent behavior departs from the dominant trend of the dataset.






TipChoosing the hypothesis



Use slope different from zero when the objective is to identify proteins showing a significant temperature-dependent abundance change.
Use slope different from the average trend when the objective is to identify proteins whose thermal behavior is unusual relative to the overall proteome response.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Limma results
The Limma results table summarizes the statistical analysis for each protein.
The results include the estimated temperature-associated effect together with the corresponding statistical significance.
Adjusted p-values are calculated to account for multiple testing.






NoteSelecting proteins from the results table



Selecting proteins in the Limma results table highlights the corresponding proteins in the volcano plot.
This provides a convenient way to investigate proteins of interest directly from the statistical results.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Limma volcano plot
The volcano plot summarizes the magnitude and statistical significance of the temperature-associated effects.






Figure 2: Volcano plot.



The X-axis represents:
logFC
and the Y-axis represents:
-log10(adjusted p-value)
A horizontal dashed line indicates an adjusted p-value threshold of:
0.05
Proteins with stronger statistical evidence appear higher on the plot.
The position along the X-axis represents the direction and magnitude of the estimated temperature-associated effect.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Quantile cutoff
The quantile cutoff percentage determines the lower and upper logFC thresholds used to classify proteins in the volcano plot.
For example, with the default setting:
5%
the lower threshold corresponds to the 5th percentile of the logFC distribution and the upper threshold corresponds to the 95th percentile.
Proteins are classified as:

Downregulated when their logFC is below the lower cutoff and adjusted p-value is below 0.05;
Upregulated when their logFC is above the upper cutoff and adjusted p-value is below 0.05;
No significant otherwise.

The quantile cutoff can be adjusted between 0 and 50%.






NoteQuantile-based classification



The quantile cutoff controls the visual classification of proteins in the volcano plot.
The significance classification therefore depends on both the adjusted p-value and the position of the protein within the observed logFC distribution.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Protein labels
The Number of top proteins to label (by logFC) control determines how many proteins are automatically labelled at each extreme of the significant logFC distribution.
For example, the default value:
10
labels up to 10 proteins with the highest significant logFC values and up to 10 proteins with the lowest significant logFC values.
This facilitates rapid identification of proteins showing the largest temperature-associated effects.

title: Model Fitting
section: Highlighting clusters in the volcano plot
text:
Highlighting clusters in the volcano plot
If clustering has previously been performed, TPP Analyst can integrate the clustering results into the Limma volcano plot.






Figure 3: Clustering integration.



Three options may be available:

None
Clusters
Sub-clusters

The available options depend on whether clustering or sub-clustering results have already been generated.

None
With None selected, proteins are colored according to their volcano-plot classification:

upregulated;
downregulated;
not significant.



Clusters
Select Clusters to color proteins according to the cluster assignments generated in the Clustering module.
This allows statistical results from Limma to be interpreted in the context of the thermal-profile groups identified during clustering.


Sub-clusters
Select Sub-clusters to highlight proteins according to their sub-cluster assignments.
Proteins that do not belong to the available sub-cluster result are displayed separately.






TipIntegrating clustering and Limma



Cluster highlighting can help determine whether proteins displaying significant temperature-associated effects are concentrated within particular thermal-profile clusters identified during exploratory analysis.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Highlighting selected proteins
Proteins manually selected in the Limma results table are emphasized in the volcano plot.
Selected proteins are shown as larger orange points and are labelled using their protein accession.
This highlighting is independent of the general volcano-plot color scheme and can therefore be used together with cluster or significance coloring.

title: Model Fitting
section: Requirement: normalization to the lowest temperature
text:
Requirement: normalization to the lowest temperature
Melting curve fitting requires the datasets to be normalized to their lowest-temperature measurements.
