Before running the analysis, ensure that:
Normalize to lowest temperature
has been applied in the Normalization module.
For analyses involving multiple datasets, lowest-temperature normalization must have been applied to all datasets.






ImportantLowest-temperature normalization is required



TPP Analyst does not run the melting curve analysis if the datasets have not been normalized to the lowest temperature.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Complete protein profiles
Melting curves are fitted using proteins with complete quantitative profiles.
Proteins containing missing measurements in the input used for curve fitting are excluded before model fitting.






NoteMissing measurements



The availability of proteins for melting curve fitting depends on the QC and normalization decisions made in previous sections.
Review missing-value handling and filtering before fitting the curves if a large number of proteins are unavailable.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Sigmoidal melting model
TPP Analyst fits a sigmoidal curve that describes the change in relative protein abundance across the temperature gradient.
The fitted parameters characterize different aspects of the thermal profile.

Melting temperature (Tm)
The melting temperature (Tm) represents the estimated midpoint of the fitted thermal transition.
Tm is one of the principal parameters used in classical thermal proteome profiling analysis.


k
The k parameter controls the shape and steepness of the fitted transition.
It contributes to the calculation of the curve slope.


Plateau (p)
The plateau (p) parameter represents the lower asymptotic abundance of the fitted melting curve.


R²
R² describes how closely the fitted sigmoidal curve represents the observed protein measurements.
Higher R² values indicate closer agreement between the fitted model and the observed thermal profile.


Slope
The slope provides a measure of the steepness of the fitted melting transition.


Area under the curve
The AUC summarizes the observed protein abundance across the measured temperature range.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Initial values for nonlinear fitting
Nonlinear model fitting requires initial estimates for the model parameters.
TPP Analyst provides two approaches:

Program estimation
Manually specified

title: Model Fitting
text:
Program estimation
Program estimation automatically determines starting values from each protein profile.
The initial estimates are based on the measured abundance values and are used as starting points for nonlinear optimization.
The program-estimated starting values include:

Tm estimated from the temperature associated with an abundance close to the median profile value;
k initialized according to the variability of the abundance measurements;
plateau initialized from the minimum observed abundance.







NoteStarting values are not final fitted values



The automatically estimated values are used only to initialize nonlinear curve fitting. The final Tm, k, and plateau values are determined by the fitted model.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Manually specified starting values
Select:
Manually specified
to provide custom initial values for:

Tm
k
p (plateau)







Figure 5: Manual starting values.



These values are used as starting guesses for the nonlinear fit.
They do not constrain the final fitted parameters to the manually supplied values.






TipManual starting values



Manual initialization can be useful when automatic starting values do not provide satisfactory convergence for a dataset with unusual thermal profiles.
For most datasets, program estimation provides a convenient starting point.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Running melting curve fitting
After configuring the starting-value method and quality filters, click:
Run melting curve fitting
TPP Analyst fits the sigmoidal model to the protein profiles and calculates the corresponding fitting parameters.
The fitting process is performed independently for each protein.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Curve quality filters
After curve fitting, proteins are filtered using five user-defined criteria:

R²
Slope
Plateau
Minimum Tm
Maximum Tm

Only proteins satisfying all selected criteria are retained in the melting curve results table and downstream Tm summaries.

title: Model Fitting
text:
R² threshold
The:
Filter: R² ≥
control defines the minimum fit quality accepted by TPP Analyst.
The default value is:
0.7
Only proteins with an R² value equal to or greater than this threshold are retained.
Increasing the threshold applies a more stringent curve-quality requirement.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Slope threshold
The:
Filter: slope ≤
control defines the maximum accepted fitted slope.
The default value is:
-0.06
Only proteins satisfying the selected slope threshold are retained.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Plateau threshold
The:
Filter p ≤
control limits the maximum accepted plateau value.
The default value is:
0.2
Proteins with fitted plateau values above the selected threshold are excluded from the displayed results.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Tm range
The estimated melting temperature can be restricted using:
Filter: Tm ≥
and:
Filter: Tm ≤
The default range is:
30°C to 95°C
Only fitted proteins with Tm estimates inside the selected interval are retained.






TipQuality filters



R², slope, plateau, and Tm filters should be considered together.
These filters allow poorly fitted or biologically implausible thermal profiles to be excluded before Tm estimates are used in downstream comparisons.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Updating curve filters
Curve-fitting filters are interactive.
After the filtering controls are changed, TPP Analyst updates the accepted protein set without requiring all melting curves to be fitted again.
A short delay is applied after changing filter settings before the displayed results are updated.






NoteFitting versus filtering



Run melting curve fitting performs the computationally intensive curve-fitting step.
Changing the R², slope, plateau, or Tm thresholds subsequently changes which fitted proteins are retained without requiring the original nonlinear fitting procedure to be repeated.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Selecting an individual protein
Select a protein directly from the melting curve results table to display its thermal profile.
Only one protein is selected at a time.
The selected protein is displayed in the Melting curve plot.






Figure 6: Melting curve plot.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Melting curve plot
The melting curve plot displays the experimental measurements for the selected protein together with its fitted sigmoidal curve.
Individual replicate measurements are distinguished using different point shapes and colors.
The X-axis represents:
Temperature (°C)
and the Y-axis represents protein:
Intensity
The fitted sigmoidal curve provides a visual representation of how well the model describes the measured thermal profile.






TipInspect individual fits



Summary parameters such as R² are useful for automated filtering, but individual melting curves should also be visually inspected when evaluating proteins of particular biological interest.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Melting temperature distribution
The Melting temperature distribution plot compares the accepted Tm estimates across the available datasets.






Figure 7: Melting temperature distribution.



For each dataset, individual protein Tm values are displayed together with a boxplot summarizing their distribution.
Only proteins whose fitted curves satisfy the currently selected R², slope, plateau, and Tm filters contribute to the distribution.
This visualization provides a global overview of protein thermal stability across the analyzed datasets.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Shared proteins
Enable:
Show only shared proteins
to restrict the Tm distribution to proteins with accepted curve fits shared across the relevant datasets.
This provides a more directly comparable set of protein Tm estimates when examining multiple experimental conditions.






NoteQuality filters and shared proteins



A protein must first pass the current melting-curve quality criteria to be included in the Tm distribution.
The shared-protein option further restricts the visualization to proteins represented across the compared datasets.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Interpreting Tm distributions
Differences in the overall Tm distributions can provide an overview of thermal stability across datasets.
However, global Tm distributions do not by themselves identify statistically significant protein-specific thermal stability changes.
Protein-level comparisons between experimental conditions are performed in the downstream comparison analyses.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Recommended Limma workflow
A typical Limma analysis is:

Select the desired null hypothesis.
Review the Limma results table.
Inspect the adjusted p-values and estimated effects.
Set the desired quantile cutoff for volcano-plot classification.
Choose how many proteins should be labelled.
Highlight clusters or sub-clusters when previous clustering results are available.
Select proteins of interest directly from the results table when needed.
Inspect the corresponding highlighted proteins in the volcano plot.
Download the volcano plot when required.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Recommended melting curve workflow
A typical melting curve fitting workflow is:

Ensure all relevant datasets have been normalized to the lowest temperature.
Select program-estimated or manually specified starting values.
Choose the initial R², slope, plateau, and Tm filtering criteria.
Click Run melting curve fitting.
Review the number of proteins passing the selected quality filters.
Inspect the fitted parameter values in the results table.
Adjust the quality filters if necessary.
Select proteins of interest and inspect their individual fitted curves.
Inspect the Tm distribution across datasets.
Enable shared proteins when a directly comparable protein set is required.
Download relevant plots for reporting or further interpretation.







ImportantModel fitting and downstream analyses



The quality of fitted thermal profiles directly affects the interpretation of the estimated melting temperatures.
Use the available fit-quality parameters together with visual inspection of representative protein curves before interpreting Tm values or using fitted proteins in downstream comparisons.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Next step
After fitting and evaluating protein thermal profiles, continue to Protein Plots for detailed visualization of individual proteins.

title: Getting Started
text:
TPP Analyst provides an integrated workflow for the analysis and visualization of quantitative Thermal Proteome Profiling (TPP) data.
This section provides an overview of the analysis workflow and the main steps required to begin an analysis.

title: Getting Started
text:
Analysis workflow
A typical TPP Analyst analysis consists of the following steps:

Prepare and load the input data
Perform quality control
Normalize the protein abundance data
Explore thermal profiles using clustering
Fit linear or sigmoidal models to the data
Visualize individual protein thermal profiles
Perform Gene Ontology analysis on clusters and limma results
Compare thermal stability profiles between experimental conditions using NPARC or TPP R methods

Each analysis module builds upon the processed data generated in the previous stages.

title: Getting Started
text:
Starting an analysis
An analysis begins by providing the protein abundance data together with an experimental design describing the corresponding experimental conditions, temperatures, and replicates.
The application supports both single-organism and multi-organism experiments.
Once the files have been loaded, TPP Analyst validates their structure and generates the datasets used throughout the downstream analysis.
Detailed input requirements are described in the Input Data section.

title: Getting Started
text:
Example datasets
TPP Analyst includes the Staurosporine thermal proteome profiling dataset from the landmark study by Savitski et al. (Science, 2014, DOI: 10.1126/science.1255784). as example dataset that can be loaded directly from the application.
The dataset allow users to explore the available analysis modules and become familiar with the expected workflow without uploading their own data.

title: Getting Started
text:
Navigating the application
The different analysis modules can be accessed through the TPP Analyst interface.
Results generated during quality control and normalization are propagated to the downstream analysis modules, allowing the complete analysis to be performed within the same application.

title: Getting Started
text:
Next step
Continue to the Input Data section to learn how to prepare and upload data for analysis.

title: GO Analysis
text:
The GO Analysis section provides tools for investigating the biological functions associated with proteins identified during TPP analysis.
TPP Analyst provides two complementary Gene Ontology enrichment approaches:
ORA evaluates whether particular Gene Ontology terms are represented more frequently within protein clusters than expected from the background protein set.
GSEA instead evaluates whether proteins associated with particular GO terms tend to occur toward the top or bottom of a ranked protein list.
The two approaches therefore answer related but different biological questions.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Fetching UniProt annotations
When organism annotation data are not already available, TPP Analyst can retrieve GO information for the proteins in the clustered dataset.
Click:
Fetch data






Figure 1: Fetching annotations



to retrieve the required protein annotation information.
The protein accessions from the current clustered dataset are used for this process.






NoteAnnotation retrieval



Fetching GO information is required only when the corresponding organism annotation data are not already available to the application or not provided by the user when loading the datasets.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Requirement: clustering
ORA requires protein cluster assignments.
Before running ORA, first complete the Clustering analysis.
The proteins assigned to each cluster are used as the target protein sets for enrichment analysis.






ImportantClustering is required



Run the Clustering section before performing ORA.
ORA uses the protein clusters generated during clustering as the groups tested for functional enrichment.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Background protein set
The background for ORA consists of the unique protein accessions available in the clustered dataset.
Each individual cluster is then compared against this background.
This allows enrichment results to be interpreted relative to the proteins available in the analyzed experiment.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Selecting a cluster
Use:
Select cluster to analyze
to choose the cluster whose ORA results should be displayed.
Available choices depend on the number of clusters generated during clustering.
For example:
Cluster 1
Cluster 2
Cluster 3
Cluster 4
The enrichment analysis is calculated for the available clusters, while the selector determines which cluster is displayed in the result table and plots.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Running ORA
After clustering and GO annotations are available, click:
Run ORA
to perform enrichment analysis.






Figure 2: Running ORA



The proteins belonging to each cluster are tested against the GO annotation database using the configured statistical parameters.
Results are then available for individual clusters through the cluster selector.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Multiple-testing correction
The:
p-value adjustment method
determines how p-values are corrected for multiple hypothesis testing.
Available options include:
BH
holm
hochberg
hommel
bonferroni
BY
fdr
none
The default method is:
BH






NoteMultiple GO terms are tested



GO enrichment analysis evaluates many terms simultaneously. Multiple-testing correction helps control the statistical error associated with performing many enrichment tests.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Minimum gene set size
The:
Minimum gene set size
determines the minimum number of annotated proteins required for a GO term to be considered during enrichment analysis.
The default value is:
10
GO terms containing fewer proteins than this threshold are excluded.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Maximum gene set size
The:
Maximum gene set size
defines the maximum number of annotated proteins allowed for a GO term.
The default value is:
500
Terms exceeding this limit are excluded from the enrichment analysis.
These minimum and maximum thresholds can be used to avoid testing gene sets that are either very small or extremely broad.

title: GO Analysis
text:
P-value cutoff
The:
p-value cutoff
defines the significance threshold used during ORA.
The default value is:
0.05

title: GO Analysis
text:
Q-value cutoff
The:
q-value cutoff
provides an additional significance threshold for enrichment results.
The default value is:
0.2

title: GO Analysis
text:
Expand GO hierarchy
The:
Expand GO hierarchy (buildGOmap)
option is enabled by default.
When enabled, TPP Analyst expands the protein-to-GO associations through the Gene Ontology hierarchy.
This propagates annotations to related parent GO terms, increasing the coverage of the enrichment database.






TipGO hierarchy expansion



Enable Expand GO hierarchy when enrichment should consider the hierarchical relationships between GO terms.
Because parent GO categories are generally broader than their descendant terms, hierarchy expansion can increase annotation coverage while also producing broader functional enrichment results.
This option will considerably increase the loading time for the enrichment database, especially for organisms with large annotation sets.

title: GO Analysis
text:
GO ontology categories
TPP Analyst determines whether enriched terms belong to:

BP: Biological Process
CC: Cellular Component
MF: Molecular Function

The GO description associated with each identifier is retrieved from the Gene Ontology annotation resources used by the application.

title: GO Analysis
text:
ORA dotplot
The Dotplot summarizes the enriched GO terms identified for the selected cluster.






Figure 3: ORA Dotplot



The plot provides a compact overview of significant functional categories and their enrichment characteristics.
Only results containing GO terms with adjusted p-values below:
0.05
are displayed.
If no terms satisfy this criterion, TPP Analyst displays:
No enriched terms found

title: GO Analysis
text:
Enrichment map
The Enrichment plot displays relationships between enriched GO terms based on their similarity.






Figure 4: Enrichment map



The enrichment map is useful for identifying groups of related functional categories rather than interpreting every enriched GO term independently.
At least three significant GO terms are required to generate the enrichment map.
If fewer than three significant terms are available, TPP Analyst displays:
Enrichment map requires at least 3 significant GO terms.






TipInterpreting related GO terms



GO enrichment frequently produces several related or partially overlapping terms.
The enrichment map can help reveal broader functional themes represented by groups of related GO categories.

title: GO Analysis
text:
ORA Upset plot
The Upset plot visualizes overlap between the protein sets associated with enriched GO terms.






Figure 5: Upset plot



This can help identify proteins contributing to multiple enriched biological categories.
As with the other ORA visualizations, the plot requires significant enrichment results with adjusted p-values below 0.05.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Ranking proteins
TPP Analyst provides two ranking metrics:

t-statistic
logFC

The ranking statistic determines the order of proteins provided to GSEA.






Figure 6: Run GSEA

title: GO Analysis
text:
t-statistic
The:
t-statistic
option ranks proteins according to the t-statistic obtained from the Limma analysis.
This is the recommended ranking method in the interface.
Because the t-statistic incorporates both effect magnitude and its estimated variability, it provides a statistical ranking of the temperature-associated protein responses.

title: GO Analysis
text:
logFC
The:
logFC
option ranks proteins according to the estimated effect generated by the Limma analysis.
This option is intended for appropriately normalized or transformed data.






WarninglogFC and raw intensity data



When logFC values appear to remain on a raw-intensity scale, TPP Analyst displays a warning recommending either:

t-statistic ranking; or
normalization/log transformation before using logFC.

For this reason, t-statistic is the recommended default ranking method.

Minimum gene set size

5

Maximum gene set size

GSEA p-value cutoff

title: GO Analysis
text:
Exponent
The Exponent controls the weighting applied to the ranked protein list during enrichment score calculation.
The default value is:
1
The interface allows values from 0 to 5.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Number of permutations
The number of permutations controls the permutation-based estimation performed during GSEA.
The default value is:
10,000
The application allows values from:
10,000 to 500,000
in increments of:
10,000






WarningNumber of permutations



Increasing the number of permutations can increase computation time considerably.
Use larger values when additional statistical stability is required and the additional computational cost is acceptable.

title: GO Analysis
text:
GSEA GO hierarchy expansion
The:
Expand GO hierarchy (buildGOmap)
option determines whether protein annotations are propagated through the GO hierarchy before GSEA.
The option is enabled by default.
As in ORA, hierarchy expansion can increase annotation coverage while also introducing broader parent GO categories into the analysis.

title: GO Analysis
text:
GSEA Upset plot
The Upset plot summarizes overlap among proteins associated with enriched GO terms.






Figure 7: GSEA Upset plot.



This helps identify proteins contributing to several functionally enriched categories.
If no terms have an adjusted p-value below 0.05, the application reports:
No enriched terms found

title: GO Analysis
text:
Ridge line plot
The Ridge line plot displays the distribution of ranked protein values associated with enriched GO terms.






Figure 8: GSEA Ridge line plot.



The plot provides a comparative overview of where proteins belonging to different functional categories occur within the ranked protein list.
This can help distinguish GO terms whose associated proteins show different distributions across the ranking statistic.

title: GO Analysis
section: Running score and preranked list plot
text:
Running score and preranked list plot
The Running score and preranked list plot provides a detailed visualization of individual GSEA results.






Figure 9: GSEA Running score and preranked list plot.



After GSEA has been performed, significant GO terms become available in:
Select term(s) to display
The selector can be searched using the GO term description.
Multiple significant terms can be selected simultaneously.
The resulting plot displays the enrichment running score across the ranked protein list for the selected GO sets.






TipExamining individual GO terms



Use the running-score plot when a particular biological process, molecular function, or cellular component is of special interest.
The searchable term selector makes it possible to move from the global enrichment overview to individual GO terms.

title: GO Analysis
text:
Significant terms available for plotting
The term selector contains GO terms with adjusted p-values below:
0.05
GO descriptions are displayed in the selector when available, while the corresponding GO identifiers are used internally for plotting.
This allows enriched terms to be located using their biological descriptions rather than GO identifiers alone.
